title: The Third Founding Declaration
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/james-davison-hunter
text:
In the annals of history, modern democracy stands out as one of humanity’s greatest achievements. From its beginnings, democracy was an exercise in hope—hope that the world and the lot of ordinary people could be made better. This was especially true in America, a nation predicated solely on the ideal of expanding freedom, equality, justice, and toleration rather than on established traditions, inherited identities, or long-standing territorial boundaries. The hope of America was for a home and a shared endeavor where Americans of all backgrounds could flourish. Both flawed and incomplete in its implementation, democracy in America—civic, pluralist, and liberal—has nevertheless stumbled forward in its history toward the realization of that ideal.

Today, however, American democracy faces its greatest crisis since the American Civil War. The signs are everywhere: extreme partisanship making political compromise impossible, increasing threats and acts of political violence, a loss of trust in all branches of government and all major institutions of civil society, and a growing disregard for the rule of law by a leadership class often defined by corruption and cowardice. These are some of the forces that today undermine the rich legacies of freedom for which Americans have sacrificed, fought, and died, forces that would ultimately pull the nation into tyranny.

Too many Americans today believe that the cause of this crisis lies in the malice of the “other side.” While active political harms are inflicted by actors across the political spectrum, the sources of our crisis trace to sources of disaffection and disempowerment with origins far deeper in American history and culture. These sources have weakened the ethical ideals, moral dispositions, and social habits that comprise America’s true constitution, one etched within the deepest aspirations of its citizens rather than merely written on parchment or graven on tablets of marble or brass.

The Call for a Third Founding

The Third Founding Declaration is a response to this crisis. It is a summons to action, no more audacious than is required by the gravity of this moment: that America cannot survive without a revival of our constitution in the fullest sense, a rededication to a common civic, pluralist, and liberal democratic project and the renewal of the ideals that animate that project.

The United States has already experienced two great Foundings. The first was the American Revolution of 1776 and the ratification of the Constitution of 1788 that together transformed thirteen British Colonies into a free and independent nation. Through it, the Founders launched the American experiment, for the first time creating a nation that would find its governing authority in the people.

The Second Founding began in the wake of the American Civil War, when Union victory meant that the liberal-egalitarian creed would be the country’s fundamental organizing idea going forward, the basis for state legitimacy, and the supreme political and cultural value binding the nation together.

The First and Second Foundings came about when it became clear that the old symbolic and cultural orders could no longer hold up in the face of profound cultural, moral, economic, and technological changes. Both were ultimately precipitated by bloody and destructive wars.

We believe that changes of a similar order are occurring around us today, and we fear that these changes will give rise to a third violent founding struggle. Already we have experienced five decades of bitter culture war, growing harsher and more violent over time, with both sides drawn to extremism and intolerance. 

The call for a Third Founding, then, is a constructive endeavor, focused on the hard work that lies ahead for all Americans within their civic institutions to deliberate, honestly and generously, the meaning of freedom, justice, equality, and toleration, particularly in relation to the thorniest issues that divide our nation. It is also a nonpartisan endeavor that takes no side other than the side of those citizens—conservative, moderate, and progressive—who see themselves as Americans first before they see themselves as Republicans, Democrats, or Independents.

A Call to Defend: Accountability

Though at its heart constructive, the call for a Third Founding is necessarily a call to defend and preserve American democracy against all forms of political violence, against the extremism that will allow neither deliberation nor compromise, against the authoritarian and autocratic forces that would impose their rule repressively, and against the reckless disregard for the rule of law and the independence of not only governmental institutions but also the civic institutions that provide the animating dynamism of a vital democratic nation.

A Call to Renew: Four Commitments

The call to a Third Founding is also, necessarily, a call to renew a civic culture that will underwrite and sustain democracy through times of extraordinary change. That work will bear fruit if it is rooted in at least four enduring commitments.

A commitment to reconstitute a civic culture centered on an ethics of human dignity and respect. If we are to achieve the aim of consolidating the moral and political goods of democracy, resisting the nihilism of our political culture, and rebuilding national solidarity around a vision of human flourishing, we must start with a moral imaginary rooted in an ethics of human dignity that is spacious enough but also grounded enough to be credible amid the fragmentation of belief and practice that, in part, has given rise to this crisis. An ethics of human dignity is foundational to any possibility of a restoration of American democracy.
Built upon this, a commitment to reaffirm the social practices within civic life befitting democratic citizens. Restoring the possibility of common action across social and political differences must begin below the level of politics, in the everyday practices that form the groundwork of social and political life. None of these is more important than the practice of civil discourse. Democracy, after all, is an agreement not to do violence to each other over our differences but to work through them dialogically. But democracy can make progress in these ways only if democratic practice operates within shared norms: a commitment to truth, because truth is, among other things, a prerequisite of justice; a commitment to toleration and civility, because these are prerequisites to peaceful coexistence; and a commitment to a discourse aimed at and justified by its promotion of common goods rather than factional interests alone. Without these norms, public and political discourse become tools of manipulation, propaganda, and demagoguery. 
A commitment to the independence and renewal of the institutions of civil society and key agencies of the government. Among the chief deformations of American democracy today are those resulting from the politicization of civil society and its various institutions, among them religion, philanthropy, education, science, journalism, the arts, professional associations, and the like, not to mention key agencies of government. When these institutions become politicized, the public is deprived of meaningful access to vital public goods and citizens become alienated from those institutions. Trust deteriorates; legitimacy erodes. By reorienting themselves around the pursuit of the internal goods that only these institutions can provide, they will lower the temperature of political conflict and restore public trust in the efficacy of these institutions.
A commitment to the renewal of democratic agency. To many, the federal government, as a whole and in its parts, seems distant, opaque, and incomprehensible. The power of government is not exercised for people but on people and through them by means of regulation, administration, education, and surveillance. A robust, functional democracy, however, embodies a humane faith in the dignifying capacity of ordinary people to deliberate over their own good, as both private individuals and members of a citizen public. The decline of that faith has been responsible for much of the discontent and the sense of powerlessness that trouble our country today. A reassertion of proper democratic limits and control over the machinery of government, coupled with the growth of a humane civic ethos that transcends the culture war, would help to restore Americans’ sense of peoplehood.

We are convinced that these ethical commitments accord with the highest ideals of American character and even today can be found in people of all convictions and persuasions.

The Call for Leadership

To defend democracy and rebuild the nation, our hope rests less with politicians or parties than with the culture-producing institutions of civil society. It is these institutions that bear the burden of leadership. These institutions—local, regional, and national—must hold the line against any and all authoritarian tendencies in the government that would subvert the rule of law, undermine the independence of civic institutions, weaken the balance of powers in government, justify political violence, or denigrate fellow citizens. They must also bear the long-term burden of modeling and promoting the civic, pluralist, and liberal ideals that have long generated cohesion in American life.

A New Era of Nation Building

America is not just a plot of land on which we live but a home that we share. Its Founding documents are not relics but blueprints for an ideal wanting to be realized. Citizenship, therefore, is not just about the rights we possess but an array of responsibilities we bear to contribute to the task of defending, caretaking, and restoring. This nation, then, is not something we inherit fully formed but something we build together, repair, and add to over generations. In this way, America becomes a place of belonging, where we not only toil for personal survival but labor toward collective flourishing. Our task is not just to live in America but to live up to it and to work together toward the realization of its promise.

This has always been America’s story, but it is a story that has gradually faded from memory, with the consequence that far too many Americans no longer experience America as a home but as a strange and inhospitable land.

To restore a national home, we must do more than legislate; we must remember, re-narrate, and renew our commitment to this home we call America. Only then can we recognize each other not as isolated individuals but as coauthors of a common story—one with a complicated history, to be sure, but one with chapters yet to be written.

We Americans now stand at a historical crossroads that requires us to make a choice: to accept an encroaching despotic rule from above or to launch an active and constructive re-founding—reclaiming the American democratic ideal adequate to the times in which we live.

That work will be long and difficult, but bracing. The illiberal and anti-democratic actors in our midst may have the loudest voices in politics and social life today, but they are in fact minority voices. The majority of Americans have become weary of their dehumanizing projects. It is time to repudiate those strategies in the name of a fundamental reconstitution, a Third Founding of the ideals and aspirations of American democracy—not, perhaps, as the world-spanning empire that she has sometimes desired to become but as a decent, flourishing, healthy political order that honors human dignity and human difference and that allows people of all sorts to thrive and prosper, each under his or her own vine and fig tree, with none to make them afraid.
